runs.text: 1. What is a daemon thread in Java?
A daemon thread is a background/helper thread whose purpose is to support the main work performed by other threads. It does not
keep the Java application running after all user threads have finished.
2. What is the difference between a primary thread and a daemon thread in this lesson?
The primary thread performs the main application task. A daemon thread performs supporting work
for that primary task. In the cricket example, Gill represents the primary worker, while the batting coach and bowling coach are helper threads.
3. Why are daemon threads used?
They are useful for background work that is needed while the main application w
ork is active. When the user threads finish, the JVM does not need to stay alive only to keep daemon threads running.
4. What real-world example is used to explain daemon threads?
A cricket team is used as an analogy. The main player, Gill, is the primary
worker. The batting coach and bowling coach support him during practice, so they represent daemon/helper threads.
5. What tasks does the primary thread perform in the cricket example?
Gill checks the pitch and ground conditions, warms up, practices catchin
g, practices batting, practices bowling, and then finishes the practice session and goes to the hotel.
6. What work do the batting coach and bowling coach perform?
They support Gill during practice. The batting coach helps with batting-related practice, an
d the bowling coach helps with bowling-related practice. Their work is secondary to Gill’s main activity.
7. How does the example represent a helper thread that remains available?
The coach threads use a repeating loop to represent being available to help
while Gill is practicing. The example uses a loop and a delay so the helper activity can run repeatedly alongside the primary task.
8. Why is Thread.sleep() used in the cricket example?
Thread.sleep() is used to create a time gap between activities. It rep
resents actions such as inspecting the pitch, taking a water break, or pausing before moving to the next practice activity.
9. How many milliseconds are equal to three seconds?
Three seconds are equal to 3,000 milliseconds. Therefore, Thread.sleep(3000)
pauses the current thread for approximately three seconds.
10. What happens when a primary/user thread finishes while daemon threads are still running?
When all user threads have finished, the JVM can exit even if daemon threads are still executing. The da
emon threads do not keep the application alive by themselves.
11. Why should the coach threads be daemon threads in this example?
The coaches exist only to help Gill. When Gill finishes his practice, the coaching threads should not keep the application run
ning independently. Marking them as daemon threads gives them that helper lifecycle.
12. What could happen if the coach threads were ordinary user threads with infinite loops?
They could keep the application running even after Gill finishes, because the JV
M waits while user threads are still alive. A continuously running helper thread should therefore be marked as daemon when it is intended to end with the application’s user work.
13. Which Java class is used to create the threads in the demonstrated exampl
e?
The example creates thread classes by extending the Thread class and overriding the run() method. The Gill, BattingCoach, and BowlingCoach objects each represent a thread.
14. What are the steps for designing daemon threads?
First, identify the primary

thread. Second, identify which supporting threads should behave as daemon threads. Third, have the primary application flow create the helper thread objects. Fourth, mark the helper threads as daemon before starting them.
15. Why should the primary thread
be identified first?
A daemon thread exists to support some primary work. Identifying the primary thread makes it clear which activity the helper threads are supporting and when their work should no longer be required.
16. Which thread creates the helper t
hread objects in the example?
The main application flow creates the Gill, BattingCoach, and BowlingCoach thread objects. It then assigns meaningful names and configures the coach threads before starting them.
17. Which method marks a thread as a daemon thr
ead?
The Thread class provides the setDaemon(boolean on) method. Calling setDaemon(true) marks the thread as a daemon thread.
18. When must setDaemon(true) be called?
It must be called before the thread is started. Configure the daemon status first, and ca
ll start() afterward.
19. What happens if setDaemon(true) is called after start()?
Java throws an IllegalThreadStateException. The daemon status cannot be changed after the thread has been started.
20. Does setDaemon(true) start the thread?
No. It only mar
ks the thread as a daemon. The thread must still be started separately by calling start().
21. Can both the batting coach and bowling coach be daemon threads?
Yes. Both helper threads can be marked as daemon by calling setDaemon(true) on each thread object
before either one is started.
22. Why should setDaemon(true) be called before start() for both coaches?
The daemon setting must be applied while each thread is still in the new state. After start() has been called, attempting to change the daemon status
causes an IllegalThreadStateException.
23. What is the role of the garbage collector in this topic?
The garbage collector is given as an example of a built-in daemon thread in Java. It performs background memory-management work by helping reclaim objects
that are no longer reachable.
24. What is the difference between a user-defined daemon thread and a built-in daemon thread?
A user-defined daemon thread is created by the programmer, such as the batting coach and bowling coach in the example. A built-in da
emon thread, such as the garbage collector, is provided by the Java runtime.
25. Why might the output of daemon threads appear incomplete or vary between runs?
Daemon threads can be stopped when the JVM exits after the user threads finish. Because their wo
rk is background work, they may not complete every loop iteration or print every expected message before the application ends.
26. Write a Java program that creates one primary thread and two daemon helper threads.
The Gill thread performs a finite sequenc

e of practice activities. The batting coach and bowling coach repeatedly provide support. Both coach threads are marked as daemon before start() is called. The exact order of printed messages can vary because the threads execute concurrently.
Sample Input: No input
Sample Output (illus
trative; thread scheduling may change the order):
Gill is inspecting the pitch
Batting coach is assisting Gill
Bowling coach is assisting Gill
Gill is warming up
Batting coach is assisting Gill
Gill is doing batting practice
Bowling coach is assisting Gill
Gill has finished and is going to the hotel
27. Write the correct order for marking and starting a daemon thread.
Create the thread object, call setDaemon(true), and then call start(). Do not call setDaemon(true) after start().
